message.text: `misses(reasons)` filters reports by the requested corpus reason before choosing the group's first report, so one defect can qualify for several reason-specific corpora according to whichever reviewer report matches the current request.

evidence.snippet: - A group with conflicting miss reasons uses the first in-scope reason in site order, falling back to `out-of-scope`. Each defect contributes one miss. Titles that normalise to no letters or digits do not form repeat clusters.

**Matching.** Matching is mechanical first. An external finding matches a Melian finding in the same file whose lines overlap its own or lie within three lines of them. A Melian finding's `cause` evidence locations at head are its sites too, because an `affected` finding sits in a file the change did not edit, and a reviewer of the diff points at the changed line that breaks it. External findings from two reviewers at one site group the same way, so one defect counts once. One reviewer's two findings at one site stay two, as two reports from one check do. A finding with no line, or an outdated one, matches nothing until the maintainer matches it by hand. A hand match, or unmatch, is recorded as the maintainer's and overrides the mechanical one. Each external finding ends matched or external-only, and each Melian finding matched or Melian-only. In milestone 4 a `Decider` question, "do these name the same defect?", refines the mechanical match.

explanation.what: `misses(reasons)` filters reports by the requested corpus reason before choosing the group's first report, so one defect can qualify for several reason-specific corpora according to whichever reviewer report matches the current request.
explanation.whatToDo: Determine each external-only group's canonical valid report/reason in site order first, using the same precedence as `Comparison.stats()`, and only then filter groups by the requested reasons.
explanation.whyHere: The active comparison decision gives a conflicting group one canonical reason: the first in-scope reason in site order, and says each defect contributes one miss. Selecting a different report after seeing the requested reason biases the measurement corpus and lets later reports override that canonical classification.

properties.failureScenario: Two reviewers report the same defect at one site. The first report in site order is adjudicated `owned-missed`; the second is adjudicated `needs-execution`. `compare misses --reason needs-execution` filters out the first report and exports the second, while `--reason owned-missed` exports the first. The same defect therefore enters both the lens-parity and probing corpora, and the probing measurement includes a defect whose canonical group reason says reading owned it.

/** The reasons a misses file can hold: every one but `out-of-scope`, since no lens owed such a miss. */
export const exportedMissReasons = ["owned-missed", "no-owner", "needs-execution"] as const;
Measuring which routes to commit, the goldens from this week's probes and the `needs-execution` misses, is the issue's second part.

- `MELIAN_EVAL_MISSES`: a JSON array of `{ name, repo, base, head, file, rule?, alternativeRules?, fix?, lines? }`, each a `needs-execution` miss in a clone on the machine. `fix` names the commit that fixed it; `lines` is the first and last line of the defect at the head. A sighting under `rule` or any of `alternativeRules` can find the miss. A miss may leave out `rule` only when it has `lines`, and then a sighting under any rule at those lines finds it; `alternativeRules` needs a `rule`. Each rule must be one some lens of the base's `full` tier declares for the file, in either mode, so one misses file serves both and a misspelt alternative exits 2. In `lens` mode one of them must be `trust-boundary`'s. A miss is scored on the reviewing lenses' own sightings at the head, `trust-boundary`'s in `lens` mode and every lens check's in `whole`, read from the review's store level by level, because a finding merged with another lens's, or with another level's, keeps only its speaker's lines and words. An ID excludes lines, so quick and careful can sight one ID at different lines, and the verifier can refute one and uphold the other. A sighting answers the miss when the verdict holds the claim of its check, ID and level unrefuted, it sits at the file under one of the miss's rules, or any rule when it names none, and it overlaps those lines. The claim may sit in any of the verdict's groups, so a refuted one scores the miss as not found. A dismissed claim counts by its own verification, since the measurement asks whether the lens sighted the defect and the verifier let it stand, and a dismissal is a person's later call that a fresh store cannot hold. A sighting the verdict holds no claim for, a reviewing lens's claim with no sighting, or a claim the verdict holds twice, leaves that miss with no score, as a failed review does. The score follows the verdict: an unrefuted claim counts whether or not its probe was sound, and the results file is what lets a reader check. explanation.what: The new exported-reason set permits `owned-missed` and `no-owner` records in a file explicitly shaped for `MELIAN_EVAL_MISSES`.
explanation.whatToDo: Limit this export format to `needs-execution`, or introduce a separately specified corpus/measurement contract for owned and ownerless misses and amend the probing/eval design before exposing those options.
explanation.whyHere: The active probing decision and eval design define that live measurement's miss corpus as `needs-execution` misses. Feeding statically owned or ownerless defects into it changes what the probing-level route score means, while this change does not amend those baselines.

properties.failureScenario: A maintainer follows the new CLI help and runs `melian compare misses --reason owned-missed`, then supplies the result as `MELIAN_EVAL_MISSES`. `Miss.load` accepts the indistinguishable entries and the probing measurement scores a defect adjudicated as readable by an existing lens as though it were a `needs-execution` miss. The resulting probing-route recall no longer measures the corpus the active decision specifies.

message.text: The cross-round `latest` key treats an external source-reference ID as a global defect identity. That ID is only stable for replay inside a comparison: a file import can reuse `ref: A1` for a different defect in every round, while one grouped defect can also have several reviewer IDs.

evidence.snippet: - A group with conflicting miss reasons uses the first in-scope reason in site order, falling back to `out-of-scope`. Each defect contributes one miss. Titles that normalise to no letters or digits do not form repeat clusters.

- An external finding has one shape. It names its reviewer, `codex`, `claude-code`, `coderabbit`, `copilot`, or `human`, with a version. It holds the file, line range, title, body, and the reviewer's severity. It keeps a stable source reference, the time posted, and whether its thread was resolved.
- A comparison holds, for one round, the external findings, Melian's, and the matches between them, in a document in the changeset's storage.
- Importers read a pull request's review threads through GitHub's GraphQL API, filtered by author login, with CodeRabbit's `coderabbitai[bot]` first. Others read a file: Codex's adversarial review JSON, or the external-finding shape for any other local reviewer.

An external finding's ID is the first 16 hex digits of a sha256 over length-prefixed fields, as `findingId` hashes its own. A thread uses its node ID. A file uses its path and the finding's `ref`. Without a `ref`, it uses the path, the finding's file and line, its title, and a sha256 of its body. The reviewer stays out, so a later change to how reviewers are named never orphans a hand record. Problem: a finding known by its position in the file took another finding's ID when a rerun dropped one above it, and a hand match moved with the ID. Solution: a finding without a `ref` is known by what it says, so an unchanged finding keeps its ID across reruns and a changed one is new. Problem: a reviewer that titles findings generically, such as "Possible bug", gave two findings at one site one ID, and the second overwrote the first. Solution: the body's digest enters a `ref`-less finding's ID, so only findings alike in file, line, title, and body are one. A file that repeats a `ref` is `ComparisonError` `invalidFile`. The version never enters the ID, and the body enters only when the file gives no `ref`.

`comparison.import(source, imported, at)` replaces what the source last imported. A finding it no longer reports goes, unless another source still holds it, and so do the hand matches and unmatches that name it, so a re-run reviewer's file replaces its own and an edited thread updates its finding. `imports` keeps each source's IDs for that, and the CLI reports the count it stored.

explanation.what: The cross-round `latest` key treats an external source-reference ID as a global defect identity. That ID is only stable for replay inside a comparison: a file import can reuse `ref: A1` for a different defect in every round, while one grouped defect can also have several reviewer IDs.
explanation.whatToDo: Introduce a cross-round identity that distinguishes round-local file refs while carrying the full alias set of each grouped defect; only a proven stable source such as the same GitHub thread should automatically replace its earlier occurrence.
explanation.whyHere: The key therefore both overwrites unrelated misses that reuse a file ref and retains stale aliases when a later round updates another report in the same defect group. Real multi-round comparison exports can silently lose a miss, retain a stale one, or emit one defect twice.

properties.failureScenario: A local reviewer writes `claude.json` with `ref: A1` for an SQL-injection miss in r1. On r2 the same output path starts numbering at A1 again, now for a different off-by-one defect that Melian matches. Both records hash to the same external ID because file refs exclude title, body, site, and round. Lines 83 and 91 delete the r1 miss and leave none, so the export loses the SQL-injection case. Conversely, if r1 grouped IDs A and B as one defect and r2 retains only B, the A-key survives and can be exported beside B or after B was matched.

Each round record holds its base, head, mint time, owned tasks and verdict copy; range mode plays no part. A round number is for display only: within `#N`, members are numbered from 1, legacy rounds first by their head's commit date, then minted rounds by mint time, ties by round ID. The snapshot keeps the numbers until the next refresh.

explanation.what: The new offline-export sort applies `byMinting` to `MembershipCandidate`s, but those candidates carry no legacy commit `date`; every added legacy round therefore ties at `MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` and is ordered by ID rather than by its head's commit date.
explanation.whatToDo: Supply each legacy candidate's authoritative head commit date before sorting (using the same membership classification path), or preserve/store the membership order rather than applying `byMinting` to date-less candidates.
explanation.whyHere: The active exact-round decision requires legacy rounds first in head-commit-date order, then minted rounds by mint time. This change claims to reuse that membership order so the last round's miss result is authoritative, but omits the input that makes the legacy half of that order work.

properties.failureScenario: A snapshot exists, then two conclusively owned legacy rounds are discovered beyond it. The older round has ID `range-b...k0` and head date 09:00; the newer has ID `range-a...k0` and head date 10:00. Both candidates have no `mintedAt`, and `MembershipReader.candidates` supplies no `date`, so `byMinting` emits the newer `range-a...` first and the older `range-b...` last. `compare misses #N` then treats the older comparison as latest and can retain its stale miss result over the newer round's result.
